guide.summary: Unit 7 extends inference to means using t-distributions: confidence intervals and significance tests for one mean, for the mean difference in paired data, and for the difference between two independent means. Choosing between paired and two-sample procedures and checking the Normal/Large Sample condition are frequent exam targets.

sections.heading: The t-distributions
sections.body: When σ is unknown (almost always), we standardize with s and use a t-distribution with df = n − 1 for one sample. t-distributions are symmetric and centered at 0 but have heavier tails than the standard Normal, so t* > z* for the same confidence; as df increases, t approaches z. Standard error of x̄: s/√n.

sections.heading: One-sample t procedures
sections.body: Interval: x̄ ± t*·s/√n. Test: t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), df = n − 1. Conditions: Random; 10% (when sampling without replacement); Normal/Large Sample: the population is Normal, or n ≥ 30, or (for small n) a graph of the sample data shows no strong skew or outliers. When n < 30, you must actually look at the data (dotplot, boxplot) and say so. Interpret intervals and P-values exactly as in Unit 6, replacing the proportion with the mean in context.

sections.heading: Paired data
sections.body: Data are paired when each observation in one group is naturally linked to one in the other (same subject before/after, twins, matched pairs, two measurements on the same item). Compute the differences, then run a one-sample t procedure on them: parameter μ_diff, x̄_d ± t*·s_d/√n, t = (x̄_d − 0)/(s_d/√n). Check the Normal condition on the differences, not on the original data. Pairing reduces variability from differences among subjects, increasing power.

sections.heading: Two independent samples
sections.body: Interval: (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± t*·√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Test of H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0: t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). Degrees of freedom come from the calculator (Welch) or, conservatively, the smaller of n₁ − 1 and n₂ − 1. Conditions apply to each sample: independent random samples or random assignment, 10% for each, Normal/Large Sample for each. Don't pool variances on the AP exam.

sections.heading: Worked example: one-sample t interval
sections.body: A random sample of 25 batteries has a mean life of 48.2 hours with a standard deviation of 4.5 hours. With 24 degrees of freedom, t* ≈ 2.064 for 95% confidence. The interval is 48.2 ± 2.064(4.5/√25) = 48.2 ± 1.86, or (46.34, 50.06) hours. Conditions: the sample is random, 25 is less than 10% of all batteries, and the sample size is under 30, so the data should show no strong skewness or outliers in a graph.

sections.heading: Worked example: paired t test
sections.body: Eight students take a test before and after tutoring. Analyze the differences (after − before), not the two separate samples. If the mean difference is 5.0 points with a standard deviation of 4.0, then t = 5.0/(4.0/√8) ≈ 3.54 with 7 degrees of freedom, giving a one-sided P-value of about 0.005. This provides convincing evidence that tutoring improves scores for students like these, assuming the conditions are met.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students use z instead of t for means with unknown σ, treat paired data as two independent samples, and fail to check Normality for small samples.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know t-distribution, degrees of freedom, standard error, one-sample, paired, and two-sample t procedures, and robustness.

sections.heading: Comparing two means
sections.body: For two independent samples, such as test scores from two randomly assigned teaching methods, the standard error is √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), and technology calculates degrees of freedom. If the 95% interval for μ₁ − μ₂ contains 0, there is no convincing evidence of a difference. Use two-sample procedures only when the samples are independent; if each subject is measured twice or subjects are matched, use paired procedures on the differences instead.

sections.heading: Free-response connection
sections.body: Inference questions are scored on four components: identifying the correct procedure and parameters, checking conditions, performing calculations, and stating a conclusion in context. Name the procedure (one-sample t interval for μ), define the parameter in context, check random, 10%, and Normal/large sample conditions, show the formula with values, and interpret the result. Missing any component lowers the score even when the arithmetic is correct.

sections.heading: Final tip
sections.body: Always check the Normal condition for small samples.

keyTakeaways: Use t (not z) for means with unknown σ; df = n − 1.
Small samples: check a graph for strong skew or outliers.
Paired data → one-sample t on the differences.
Two independent groups → two-sample t, unpooled.
Larger n, lower confidence → narrower interval.
Conclusions about μ, in context, linked to α.
commonMistakes: Using a two-sample test on paired data.
Claiming the Normal condition is met because 'the sample is random.'
Checking Normality on the original values for paired data.
Saying 'the sample mean is likely between…' instead of the population mean.
examTips: Justify paired vs. two-sample explicitly: 'each student measured twice'.
For small n, the reader expects: 'The dotplot of the sample shows no strong skewness or outliers.'
State df and show the formula with values substituted.
Confidence-interval reasoning: is the claimed value inside the interval?
guide.cramSheet:
**One mean:** x̄ ± t*·s/√n · t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) · df = n − 1

**Conditions:** Random · 10% · Normal/Large (pop Normal, n ≥ 30, or graph OK)

**Paired:** differences → one-sample t · μ_diff

**Two-sample:** (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ± t*√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) · df from calc or min(n − 1)

**t vs z:** heavier tails · t* > z* · → z as df ↑

vocab.definition: A symmetric distribution with heavier tails than the Normal, used when σ is estimated by s.
The parameter of a t-distribution; for one sample, n − 1.
s/√n, the estimated standard deviation of x̄.
x̄ ± t*·s/√n, an interval for a population mean.
A test of H₀: μ = μ₀ using t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n).
Two measurements linked by subject or matching, analyzed through their differences.
The population mean of the paired differences.
A test comparing the means of two independent groups.
Population Normal, n ≥ 30, or sample data show no strong skew or outliers.
A procedure that gives approximately correct results even when conditions are mildly violated.
The t value that captures the central C% of a t-distribution with given df.
Formula for df in the unpooled two-sample t procedure, computed by technology.

choices.text: Nothing, because the sample is random
A graph of the sample data showing no strong skewness or outliers

practice.topic: 7.3 Justifying a Claim About a Population Mean Based on a Confidence Interval
practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval for the mean daily screen time of teens is (5.8, 7.1) hours. A report claims the mean is 7.5 hours. Which conclusion is best?

choices.text: The claim is plausible because 7.5 is close to the interval.
The interval provides convincing evidence against the claim, because 7.5 is not a plausible value.
No conclusion is possible without a test.

practice.explanation: Values outside the interval are not plausible at the 95% level.

practice.topic: 7.2 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
practice.stem: A 95% t-interval for a mean is computed from a sample of 20. If the same data were used to compute a 90% interval, the 90% interval would

choices.text: be narrower, with the same center

practice.explanation: Lower confidence uses a smaller t*; the center (x̄) doesn't change.

practice.topic: 7.4 Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean
practice.stem: A random sample of 15 house prices from a neighborhood includes one mansion priced far above all others, and a boxplot shows strong right skew. Why is a one-sample t-interval inappropriate?

choices.text: With n < 30, the strong skew and outlier suggest the population isn't Normal, so the Normal condition fails.
t-intervals require σ to be known.

practice.explanation: Small samples need roughly symmetric data without outliers.

practice.topic: 7.8 Setting Up a Test for the Difference of Two Population Means
practice.stem: To compare two tire brands, researchers put one tire of each brand on the rear wheels of 15 cars (brand assigned to left/right by coin flip) and measure tread wear. An analyst uses a two-sample t-test and finds P = 0.24. A paired t-test on the same data gives P = 0.003. Which explains the difference?

choices.text: The paired test is wrong because the samples are independent.
Pairing removes car-to-car variability (driving habits, roads), so the paired test detects the brand difference that the two-sample test misses.
The two-sample test has more power because it uses more degrees of freedom.

practice.explanation: The data are paired by car; the two-sample test incorrectly treats car variation as noise.

distractors.C: Extra df doesn't make up for ignoring pairing.

practice.topic: 7.7 Justifying a Claim About the Difference of Two Means Based on a Confidence Interval
practice.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ_A − μ_B, the difference in mean battery life (hours), is (1.2, 4.8). Which statement is correct?

choices.text: There is no evidence of a difference.
95% of brand A batteries last 1.2 to 4.8 hours longer than brand B batteries.
There is convincing evidence that brand A's mean battery life exceeds brand B's, by somewhere between 1.2 and 4.8 hours.

practice.explanation: The entire interval is positive, so A − B > 0 is supported; the interval estimates the difference in means.

practice.topic: 7.2 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
practice.stem: A student says, "Our 95% confidence interval for the mean is (12.3, 15.7), so 95% of the sample values fall in this interval." Why is this wrong?

choices.text: Confidence intervals only apply to proportions.
It should be 95% of population values.
The interval estimates the population mean, not where individual data values lie; individual values are much more spread out.

practice.explanation: Intervals for μ are based on s/√n, which is much smaller than the spread of individual values.

distractors.B: Also wrong for the same reason.

practice.topic: 7.5 Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean
practice.stem: A study with n = 4,000 finds that a new teaching method raises mean test scores by 0.4 points on a 100-point scale, with P < 0.001. Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.text: The method produces a large, important improvement.
The difference is statistically significant, but 0.4 points may not be practically important; large samples can detect tiny effects.
The result must be a Type I error.
The P-value shows that 99.9% of students improved.

practice.explanation: Statistical significance doesn't imply practical significance.

practice.topic: 7.5 Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean
practice.prompt:
A tutoring center randomly selected 10 of its students who took a practice exam, completed four weeks of tutoring, and then took a second practice exam of similar difficulty. The improvement (second score − first score) for each student was:

3, 5, −1, 4, 6, 2, 0, 7, 3, 5

A dotplot of the improvements shows no strong skewness or outliers.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why a paired t-procedure is appropriate rather than a two-sample t-procedure.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State hypotheses for testing whether students at this center improve on average, and check conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and P-value, and state a conclusion at α = 0.05.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Can the center conclude that tutoring caused the improvement? Explain.

rubric.description: Each student provides both scores, so the two measurements are linked (dependent); analyze the within-student differences.

H₀: μ_diff = 0; Hₐ: μ_diff > 0, where μ_diff = true mean improvement for all students at the center. Random sample; 10 < 10% of all students (assume the center has more than 100); dotplot of differences shows no strong skew/outliers.
x̄_d = 3.4, s_d ≈ 2.55, t = 3.4/(2.55/√10) ≈ 4.22, df = 9, P ≈ 0.001 < 0.05: reject H₀; convincing evidence of a positive mean improvement.
No: there was no control group and no random assignment; improvement could come from practice effects (taking the exam twice), studying on their own, or other factors.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Each student took both practice exams, so the two scores for a student are related. The appropriate analysis uses each student's improvement, which removes differences in ability between students; a two-sample procedure would wrongly treat the scores as independent groups.

(b) Let μ_diff be the true mean improvement (second − first) for all students at this center. H₀: μ_diff = 0; Hₐ: μ_diff > 0.
Random: the 10 students were randomly selected.
10%: it is reasonable that the center has more than 100 students.
Normal: n = 10 is small, but the dotplot of the improvements shows no strong skewness or outliers.

(c) Paired t-test: x̄_d = 3.4, s_d ≈ 2.55, n = 10. t = 3.4/(2.55/√10) ≈ 4.22 with df = 9. P-value ≈ 0.001. Because 0.001 < 0.05, we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that the true mean improvement for students at this center is greater than 0.

(d) No. This was not an experiment with a control group and random assignment. Students might improve simply from taking a similar exam a second time or from studying on their own, so we cannot attribute the improvement to tutoring.
